views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the current posture of tariffs-in-place and proposed-but-not-yet-implemented Section 301 duties while the high-level Mnuchin-Lighthizer delegation meets Liu He in Beijing this week. Do not escalate further before the talks produce a result. The US holds leverage — the economy is strong, and the ZTE denial order has demonstrated willingness to use non-tariff tools — but premature escalation risks collapsing talks that have barely begun and unifying Chinese domestic opposition.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The US economy is in a position of strength as of early May 2018: industrial production has risen from 101.5 to 102.4 over the prior six months (INDPRO), consumer sentiment stands at 98.0 (UMCSENT), and unemployment is low. The Fed is tightening (FEDFUNDS at 1.70%, up from 1.30%), reflecting confidence in growth, though the 10-year yield at 2.97% and rising Baa corporate spreads (4.80%, up from 4.24%) bear watching.

Against this backdrop, the threat to US interests is real but moderate. China's IP/tech-transfer practices are the core grievance (Section 301 report, 2018-03-22), and the $375B bilateral trade deficit is unsustainable. However, China's retaliatory tariffs on $3B of US goods (2018-04-02, targeting pork, fruit, nuts) and threatened $50B retaliation including soybeans (2018-04-04) will hurt US farm-belt constituencies. The ZTE denial order (2018-04-16) was a powerful demonstration of US leverage but has already damaged US suppliers — Acacia dropped 36%, Qualcomm lost ~10% — and risks accelerating Chinese efforts to build independent semiconductor supply chains, which would erode long-term US tech dominance.

The Beijing talks starting May 3 are the critical variable. China has signaled it will refuse to discuss the $100B deficit demand or Made in China 2025 curbs (NYT, 2018-04-30), but is offering auto tariff reductions, financial sector opening, and IP tightening. The US delegation is internally split — Mnuchin/Kudlow favoring a deal that calms markets, Lighthizer/Navarro demanding structural reform. Escalating now (e.g., implementing the $50B tariff list or expanding entity lists) before seeing what China offers would be premature. The right move is to hold, let the delegation assess China's offer, and preserve escalation as a credible next step if talks fail. The threat score of -0.2 reflects that the US has leverage and the balance of risks tilts slightly in America's favor — but only if escalation is used strategically, not reflexively.
key_factors: US economy strong: industrial production rising, consumer sentiment at 98, Fed tightening signals confidence
Section 301 $50B tariff list proposed but not yet implemented — comment period still open
China retaliated on $3B (232) and threatened $50B (301) including soybeans targeting farm-belt politics
ZTE denial order (Apr 16) demonstrates US leverage but damages US suppliers (Qualcomm -10%, Acacia -36%)
Beijing talks starting May 3 — China refuses to discuss Made in China 2025 or $100B deficit demand
US delegation split: Mnuchin/Kudlow (deal-oriented) vs Lighthizer/Navarro (structural reform hawks)
Rising corporate bond spreads (Baa at 4.80%) and 10Y yield near 3% warrant monitoring
Huawei investigation underway — potential for further non-tariff escalation

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine, and related items) in response to Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China says it will refuse to discuss Trump's two toughest trade demands: mandatory $100B deficit cut and curbs on Made in China 2025.
Qualcomm experienced 9.9% stock loss; Acacia plunged 35.97%; Oclaro and Lumentum dropped 15.18% and 9.06% respectively following ZTE ban.
US Industrial Production rose from 101.46 (Dec 2017) to 102.40 (May 2018).
Consumer Sentiment at 98.0 (May 2018), down from peak of 101.4 (March) but still elevated.
